paragraphs.text: Syndromic congenital fibrosis of extraocular muscles-3A with anosmia and developmental delay, also called the TUBB3 E410K syndrome, is caused by the recurrent E410K substitution in TUBB3. It is characterized by congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles (CFEOM3), facial weakness, developmental delay and intellectual disability, and a progressive sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Patients also have Kallmann syndrome (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia), stereotyped midface hypoplasia and, in some cases, vocal cord paralysis, tracheomalacia, and cyclic vomiting (Chew et al., 2013). Dentici et al. (2020) described the disorder as one of CFEOM3, intellectual disability, and a wide range of neurologic and endocrine abnormalities.

paragraphs.text: Tischfield et al. (2010) studied 29 unrelated families with CFEOM3 that was either isolated or accompanied by other neurologic features, and found TUBB3 mutations in them. The E410K substitution was found in 6 pedigrees. Everyone with E410K had severe CFEOM3 and congenital facial weakness. Patients with E410K had diffuse hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, a hypoplastic anterior commissure, and mild to moderate intellectual, social, and behavioral impairments. The oldest patient with E410K developed lower extremity weakness and sensory loss in the second to third decade. Across the TUBB3 mutations, brain imaging showed dysgenesis of the corpus callosum, anterior commissure, and internal capsule, with basal ganglia dysmorphisms but no cortical dysplasia or migration defect. Intellectual and behavioral impairments generally correlated with how severe the corpus callosum dysgenesis was.

paragraphs.text: Chew et al. (2013) described the detailed phenotypes of 8 unrelated individuals with the de novo TUBB3 E410K mutation. All had CFEOM, facial weakness, developmental delay, and a progressive sensorimotor polyneuropathy, which electrophysiology confirmed. The authors expanded the phenotype to include Kallmann syndrome (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia), stereotyped midface hypoplasia, and intellectual disabilities. Some patients also had vocal cord paralysis, tracheomalacia, and cyclic vomiting. On neuroimaging, the corpus callosum and anterior commissure were thin, and the olfactory sulci, olfactory bulbs, and oculomotor and facial nerves were hypoplastic to absent. Chew et al. (2013) concluded that the E410K substitution defines a new genetic cause of Moebius syndrome, Kallmann syndrome, and cyclic vomiting.

She went through normal sexual development at puberty and had 3 spontaneous pregnancies. In addition, the sons had variable features suggesting further endocrine abnormalities. The authors noted that this variability in the reproductive phenotype complicated genetic counseling.

paragraphs.text: Grant et al. (2019) performed neuropsychological testing and neuroimaging in 7 unrelated individuals with the TUBB3 E410K syndrome (4 pediatric and 3 adult). The subjects had intellectual and social disabilities despite having no cortical malformations. Compared with 22 controls, structural and diffusion MRI showed decreased corpus callosum volume and decreased network efficiency. Only the pediatric subjects had diffuse decreases in fractional anisotropy, mainly in mid- and long-range tracts. Only the adults had white matter volume loss, which was associated with decreased cortical surface area. In all subjects, the corticospinal tract had an aberrant trajectory and the long segment of the dorsal language network was absent on both sides.

paragraphs.text: Jia et al. (2022) reported 2 Chinese Han patients with the TUBB3 E410K variant. The first, a boy (C21) last examined at age 11 years, had congenital bilateral ptosis, exotropia and hypotropia, limited horizontal and vertical eye movements, corneal exposure, and facial weakness. He also had intellectual impairment, impaired gait, and cryptorchidism, and no congenital contractures. Neuroimaging showed abnormal olfactory bulbs and sulci, oculomotor nerve hypoplasia, and malformations of the corpus callosum, anterior commissure, and lateral ventricles. The second, a female (C32), had bilateral ptosis, exotropia, limited eye movements, corneal exposure, facial weakness, intellectual impairment, impaired gait, and infertility. MRI at age 19 years showed a hypoplastic corpus callosum, asymmetric lateral ventricles, absent olfactory bulbs and sulci, hypoplasia of the oculomotor nerve, and absence of both facial nerves. Both patients met the diagnostic criteria for Kallmann syndrome. The authors suggested that TUBB3 may be involved in the pathogenesis of Kallmann syndrome.
